newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya commandos to protect Chechens abroad, oil.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya commandos to protect Chechens abroad, oil.

text.p: Chechen rebel leader Aslan Maskhadov has decided to form two commando groups to help free Chechens taken hostage abroad and to thwart oil pipeline thieves at home, Interfax news agency said on Sunday.
Interfax quoted Maskhadov's spokesman Kazbek Khadzhiyev as saying decrees to this effect will be signed in the next few days.
Chechen officials had threatened to create such a force after five Chechens were briefly held hostage in the neighbouring Russian region of North Ossetia.

The captives were later freed and the Chechens are now demanding the extradition of the hostage-takers while some influential Chechen field commanders have threatened to undertake an operation to punish the North Ossetians.
"The president (Maskhadov) will personally task the group on each occasion to avoid diplomatic complications with foreign states," Khadzhiyev said.
The other group will help ensure the safety of the pipeline through which oil from Azerbaijan's off-shore deposits is expected to run to Black Sea ports in the autumn.
Chechnya and Russia, who both stand to earn generous revenues from the pipeline, are cooperating on reconstructing it. Oil traffic effectively halted at the start of the Chechnya conflict in 1994.
Analysts say a chunk of Chechnya's population in the past lived partly on stealing, processing and selling oil from the pipeline.

Apart from the North Ossetian incident there have been no reports of Chechens being taken hostage abroad, while dozens of hostages, including two Britons, a Frenchman, a Slovak and six Russian journalists, are being held in Chechnya.

Khadzhiev gave no clue to how the commandos would operate and whether missions would be coordinated with the governments of countries they might be dispatched to. Chechen officials were not available for comment.
Maskhadov last week ordered a 300-strong brigade set up to hunt for criminals and free hostages in Chechnya.
Chechen leaders, who signed a peace agreement with Moscow last August to end 21 months of bitter fighting with the Russian troops, insist that their southern region is independent from Russia.
